quests.textToSpeak: If I had more time, I'd probably learn another language.
quests.textWithBlanks: If I had more ___, I'd probably learn another language.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "time".
quests.explanation: This is a second conditional, imagining an unreal present: if I had more time. Money and help are equally grammatical, so only the audio tells you which resource the speaker is imagining.
quests.hint: A hypothetical situation that did not actually happen.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "time" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: Given how unpredictable the weather's been, everything could change by the weekend.
quests.textWithBlanks: Given how unpredictable the ___'s been, everything could change by the weekend.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "weather".
quests.explanation: Everything could change means the whole plan might shift, and any of these three nouns could reasonably follow the same warning. Given how unpredictable the weather's been sets up an uncertain conditional.
quests.hint: The direction the wind can suddenly move things.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "weather" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: As long as there's no roadworks on the way, we should be back by dark.
quests.textWithBlanks: As long as there's no ___ on the way, we should be back by dark.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "roadworks".
quests.explanation: Roadworks, diversions and the route are all things that could interfere with a plan, and all fit naturally after assuming. As long as introduces a condition the whole rest of the sentence depends on.
quests.hint: Assuming nothing unexpected gets in the way.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "roadworks" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: If it weren't for the traffic, we'd have made it on time.
quests.textWithBlanks: If it weren't for the ___, we'd have made it on time.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "traffic".
quests.explanation: If it weren't for is a fixed structure meaning because of, thanking a specific factor for preventing a worse outcome. Traffic, weather and roadworks are all realistic causes of delay, so only listening tells you which.
quests.hint: A word introducing the reason something did not happen.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "traffic" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: Even though most of the team agreed, the plan still got delayed.
quests.textWithBlanks: Even though ___ of the team agreed, the plan still got delayed.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "most".
quests.explanation: Most, half and some of the team are all real proportions, and the meeting's outcome depends entirely on which one you heard. Even though sets up a concession, so the second clause may surprise you.
quests.hint: The larger number of people in the group.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "most" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: Whatever they decide, I'm happy to go along with it.
quests.textWithBlanks: Whatever they ___, I'm happy to go along with it.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "decide".
quests.explanation: Whatever they decide, say and choose are all grammatical after this opening, and each implies a slightly different kind of decision. I'm happy to go along with signals flexibility rather than a fixed opinion.
quests.hint: Regardless of what someone else settles on doing.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "decide" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: Apparently the launch has been cancelled, though nobody's confirmed it officially.
quests.textWithBlanks: Apparently the launch has been ___, though nobody's confirmed it officially.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "cancelled".
quests.explanation: This is reported speech, so apparently signals the news came second-hand. Cancelled, delayed and postponed all fit, but the whole meaning of the sentence hinges on which one was actually said.
quests.hint: She told a colleague, who then told the speaker.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "cancelled" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: Supposedly they're merging with another company next year.
quests.textWithBlanks: ___ they're merging with another company next year.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "Supposedly".
quests.explanation: Apparently and supposedly both introduce unconfirmed information, while obviously claims certainty instead. According to whom is not stated, which is exactly what these words signal.
quests.hint: Used to introduce what someone told you, distancing yourself from it.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "Supposedly" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: From what I heard, he told her the offer wasn't final.
quests.textWithBlanks: From what I heard, he ___ her the offer wasn't final.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "told".
quests.explanation: Told, warned and reminded her all fit after he, but each carries a different tone: neutral, cautionary or gently prompting. From what I heard sets the whole sentence up as second-hand.
quests.hint: The person said something to her, and the speaker is now repeating it.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "told" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: It's cheaper to fly in winter, but it's rarely as warm.
quests.textWithBlanks: It's cheaper to fly in winter, but it's rarely as ___.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "warm".
quests.explanation: This comparison stretches across the whole sentence: cheaper doesn't automatically mean warmer, better or nicer. You need every word to know exactly what quality is actually being compared.
quests.hint: The place with better weather most days.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "warm" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: I compared a few prices, and to be honest, they're much of a muchness.
quests.textWithBlanks: I compared a few prices, and to be honest, they're much of a ___.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "muchness".
quests.explanation: Much of a muchness, more or less the same, and about the same are all idiomatic ways to say two things are similar. Comparing prices sets up an expectation, but the sentence overturns it: there is no clear winner.
quests.hint: Roughly equal, with no real difference between them.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "muchness" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: Typically, it's the least frequent route that gets cancelled first.
quests.textWithBlanks: Typically, it's the least ___ route that gets cancelled first.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "frequent".
quests.explanation: Least frequent, expensive and reliable are three different criteria for judging a bus route, and the sentence only makes sense once you know which one is being complained about. This structure requires holding the comparison in mind until the very end.
quests.hint: The service that runs less often than the others.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "frequent" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: If it comes to that, the evidence is largely in our favour.
quests.textWithBlanks: If it comes to that, the evidence is largely in our ___.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "favour".
quests.explanation: In our favour, interest and advantage are close in meaning, but favour is the idiomatic choice in this legal-sounding context. If it comes to that sets up a conditional whose outcome is still uncertain.
quests.hint: The part of the argument that would benefit us.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "favour" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: It might be worth consulting a lawyer before you sign anything.
quests.textWithBlanks: It might be worth ___ a lawyer before you sign anything.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "consulting".
quests.explanation: Consult, hire and involve a lawyer are all things a company might do, but only one is a formal recommendation typically made by a colleague. Might be worth is deliberately indirect professional advice.
quests.hint: To bring in an outside expert to help.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "consulting" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: Under the terms of the contract, they're obliged to give thirty days' notice.
quests.textWithBlanks: Under the terms of the contract, they're ___ to give thirty days' notice.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "obliged".
quests.explanation: Obliged, entitled and expected all describe your position, but obliged specifically means required by an agreement. Under the terms of the contract sets up exactly what kind of obligation is meant.
quests.hint: Legally required to do it, whether you want to or not.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "obliged" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: As far as I can tell, the root cause is a loose connection somewhere.
quests.textWithBlanks: As far as I can tell, the root ___ is a loose connection somewhere.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "cause".
quests.explanation: Root cause, main issue and real problem all name what is actually behind a symptom, and each is a common diagnostic phrase. As far as I can tell signals the speaker's honest but uncertain assessment.
quests.hint: The thing that started the trouble in the first place.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "cause" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: It's tempting to cut corners, but it usually costs more in the long term.
quests.textWithBlanks: It's tempting to cut corners, but it usually costs more in the long ___.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "term".
quests.explanation: In the long term, run and future all express roughly the same idea, but long term is the standard collocation used in planning conversations. It's tempting to signals a shortcut the speaker is warning against.
quests.hint: In the long run, over an extended period.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "term" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: Rather than replace the whole unit, they just patched it up.
quests.textWithBlanks: Rather than replace the whole unit, they just patched it ___.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "up".
quests.explanation: Patch it up, over and together all describe a partial fix, but patch it up is the idiom used when a proper repair is postponed. Rather than sets up a contrast with a more thorough alternative.
quests.hint: To do the smallest possible fix rather than the full one.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "up" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: The whole rest of the deal is fine. It's just this one sticking point.
quests.textWithBlanks: The whole rest of the deal is fine. It's just this one sticking ___.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "point".
quests.explanation: Sticking point, issue and problem are near synonyms, but sticking point specifically means the one detail negotiations are stuck on. The whole rest is fine sets up a contrast: only one part is unresolved.
quests.hint: The main obstacle that everything else depends on.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "point" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: Provided that the delivery date holds, the price stays fixed.
quests.textWithBlanks: Provided that the delivery date holds, the price stays ___.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "fixed".
quests.explanation: Fixed, final and firm all describe a price that cannot move, and each is common in negotiation. Provided that introduces a condition, so the second clause depends entirely on it being met.
quests.hint: With no room left to change anything else.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "fixed" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: Unless someone shifts, we're not going to find any common ground.
quests.textWithBlanks: Unless someone shifts, we're not going to find any common ___.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "ground".
quests.explanation: Common ground, an agreement and a compromise are three different possible outcomes of a discussion, and unless suggests the current state is uncertain. Unless someone shifts implies neither side has moved so far.
quests.hint: Neither side has given anything up yet.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "ground" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: Considering the weather, the turnout was actually pretty good.
quests.textWithBlanks: Considering the weather, the ___ was actually pretty good.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "turnout".
quests.explanation: Attendance was small, turnout was small and numbers were small all describe the same thing with different nouns, so the noun itself is what decides the sentence, not the meaning. Considering the weather offers a mitigating reason before the main point.
quests.hint: The number of people who eventually showed up.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "turnout" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: The data's actually available, but nobody seems to be using it.
quests.textWithBlanks: The data's actually ___, but nobody seems to be using it.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "available".
quests.explanation: Available, published and shared all describe data that exists somewhere, but available specifically means it can be accessed if someone bothers to look. Nobody seems to be using it is the surprising twist the sentence builds toward.
quests.hint: The information exists, but almost nobody has looked at it.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "available" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: At first glance the results look great, but the sample size is misleading.
quests.textWithBlanks: At first glance the results look great, but the sample size is ___.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "misleading".
quests.explanation: Misleading, flawed and biased all critique data in different ways: misleading suggests it creates a false impression rather than being simply wrong or one-sided. At first glance signals a claim the speaker is about to complicate.
quests.hint: Something that looks convincing but is not actually reliable.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "misleading" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: It's worth checking the restricted items list before you pack.
quests.textWithBlanks: It's worth checking the ___ items list before you pack.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "restricted".
quests.explanation: Restricted, banned and prohibited items all mean roughly the same in an airport context, but restricted is the standard sign wording. Check the list before you pack suggests advance planning is expected.
quests.hint: The list of things you are not permitted to bring on board.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "restricted" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: They actually weighed my carry-on at the gate this time.
quests.textWithBlanks: They actually weighed my ___ at the gate this time.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "carry-on".
quests.explanation: Carry-on, cabin and checked bag are all real airline terms, but only one was actually said in this sentence. Weighed my is spoken quickly, so the object arrives sooner than expected.
quests.hint: The bag you keep with you, not the one you check in.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "carry-on" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: Even though we got there early, security still took forty minutes.
quests.textWithBlanks: Even though we got there early, ___ still took forty minutes.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "security".
quests.explanation: Security, customs and passport control all involve checks before flying, but the sentence's second half about liquids points specifically to one of them. Even though signals a contrast between how early they arrived and how long the queue still took.
quests.hint: The point where you show your documents before boarding.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "security" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: I can feel my old habit of procrastinating creeping back in.
quests.textWithBlanks: I can feel my old habit of procrastinating creeping back ___.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "in".
quests.explanation: Creeping back in, up and around are three phrases with the same rough sense of returning gradually, but creeping back in is the idiomatic choice for a bad habit resurfacing. I can feel signals a slow, internal realisation rather than a sudden fact.
quests.hint: The habit of putting things off is coming back.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "in" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: Whenever I open my laptop first thing, I just stare at my to-do list.
quests.textWithBlanks: Whenever I open my laptop first thing, I just stare at my ___ list.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "to-do".
quests.explanation: To-do list, inbox and calendar are all things that can feel overwhelming, and each implies a different kind of pressure. The whole sentence is one long dependent structure, so the noun only arrives at the very end.
quests.hint: The list of things to be done, not yet started.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "to-do" fits into the spoken context.

quests.textToSpeak: Rather than trying to do everything, I just start with the smallest task.
quests.textWithBlanks: Rather than trying to do everything, I just start with the ___ task.
quests.phoneticTip: Pay close attention to initial consonants and reduced vowels when listening for "smallest".
quests.explanation: Smallest, easiest and quickest task are all reasonable strategies for getting started, and the technique described relies specifically on picking the least demanding one. Rather than sets up a contrast with tackling everything at once.
quests.hint: The one, single small task, done first.
quests.instruction: Listen to the sentence and study how "smallest" fits into the spoken context.
